title: Third declension: i-stems and adjectives

objectives.can: Parse third-declension adjectives of one, two and three endings, and i-stem nouns.

explanation.summary: Many third-declension words take the endings of the i-stems: -i in the ablative singular of adjectives, -ium in the genitive plural, -ia in the neuter plural. Third-declension adjectives are common in the Vulgate (*gravis*, *potens*, *fidelis*), and recognising their endings is the first step to seeing which noun each one belongs to.

sections.heading: Two kinds of third-declension word
body: You have met the consonant-stem nouns of the third declension, such as *rex* (stem *reg-*) and *virtus* (stem *virtut-*). A second group, the i-stems, once had a stem ending in -i and kept an extra -i- in some of its endings. The clearest sign is the genitive plural: -um for consonant stems (*regum*), -ium for i-stems (*civium*, *montium*, *ignium*).
Latin grammarians (Allen and Greenough, Bennett) sort nouns into i-stems by rules of thumb, and the rules have exceptions. A safer habit is to learn the genitive plural of each noun as you meet it.

sections.heading: Third-declension adjectives: -i in the ablative
body: An adjective of the third declension is declined like an i-stem noun, with two differences you can rely on. The ablative singular ends in -i (*gravi somno*, 'with a heavy sleep'), not -e; and the genitive plural ends in -ium. The neuter nominative and accusative plural end in -ia (*gravia*, *terribilia*).

The commonest pattern has two endings: one form serves for masculine and feminine, another for neuter (*fortis* masculine and feminine, *forte* neuter; *gravis*, *fidelis*, *humilis*, *terribilis*). Some adjectives have one ending for all genders in the nominative singular (*potens*, *prudens*, *sapiens*, *omnipotens*, *felix*) and only the stem changes: *potent-*, *prudent-*, *felic-*. A few have three endings (*acer* masculine, with feminine -is and neuter -e added to the stem *acr-*; *celer* likewise). In the library these are rare in the forms that can be taught with certainty.

head: Case
Masc. and fem.
Neuter
rows: -i (often -e when the adjective stands for a person)

sections.heading: Reading the ending, not the gender
body: In the third declension many endings are shared by two cases or by two genders. *potentes* may be nominative or accusative plural, masculine or feminine; only the sentence decides. In Luke the same word *potentes* is the object of *deposuit*, and the verse is worth keeping in mind as a reminder that the ending alone does not give the case.

The analyser used in this library says so when it cannot decide: it leaves the feature undecided rather than guess. When a question asks for a case and the word's ending fits several cases, such a word is not used. The lesson gives you the ending patterns; the clause supplies the rest.

sections.heading: Agreement
body: An adjective agrees with its noun in case, number and gender, but the endings need not rhyme. *Gravi somno* is ablative singular masculine in both words, yet the endings are -i and -o. In *onera gravia* the neuter plural noun and the neuter plural adjective do rhyme. Look for the noun an adjective goes with, then check that case and number match.

misunderstandings: An ablative singular in -i does not mean the word is dative. Third-declension adjectives have -i in the ablative as well as in the dative, so *gravi* can be either; the sentence (here a preposition such as *de*) decides.
A neuter plural in -ia is not a first-declension feminine singular. *gravia* and *terribilia* are neuter plural adjectives, nominative or accusative.
A word ending in -es is not always nominative. In the third declension -es is both nominative and accusative plural (*potentes*, *humiles*), and the analyser usually leaves the case undecided.

deeper.heading: Why -ium and -i?
body: The i-stems are older than the rule. Words with a stem in -i- (*hosti-*, *navi-*) kept the -i- before endings beginning with a vowel or -b-, and the consonant stems did not. Over time the groups mixed: some consonant-stem nouns took i-stem endings, and in late and Christian Latin the old distinctions loosen further. The Vulgate and the Fathers sometimes show -um where classical Latin has -ium, and the reverse. Grammars describe classical usage; the texts you read here are later.

quoted.english: And they told him, saying: Joseph thy son is living: and he is ruler in all the land of Egypt. Which when Jacob heard, he awaked as it were out of a deep sleep, yet did not believe them.

examples.analysis: *gravi* is a third-declension adjective, here ablative singular, and *somno* is ablative singular masculine: 'from a heavy sleep'. The adjective ends in -i, the noun in -o. They agree in case, number and gender although the endings do not match, and *de* takes the ablative.

examples.analysis: *gravia* is the neuter plural of *gravis*, nominative or accusative (the analyser does not decide). It agrees with *onera*, 'burdens', and the whole phrase is the object of *alligant*: 'they bind heavy burdens'. Neuter plural -ia is the mark of the third-declension adjective.

examples.analysis: *prudente* is ablative singular of *prudens*, an adjective with one nominative ending. The ablative ends in -e here, not -i. The -i of the ablative is the usual rule, but adjectives of this kind very often take -e when they describe a person, so treat the rule as a strong tendency, not a law. The phrase belongs to *cum proconsule Sergio Paulo viro prudente*, all in the ablative after *cum*.

examples.analysis: *ignium* is the genitive plural of *ignis*, 'fire'. The ending -ium is the sign of an i-stem noun: a consonant stem would have -um. The word depends on *receptacula*: 'receptacles of fires', that is, fire-pans.
